Right, if he wins by any margin, it's still very impressive in an objective, non-expectations-adjusted sense.

It was also stupid AF for him to release a bunch of internals showing himself +13 or whatever.

If I were a campaign manager, not only would I never release internal polls, I'd also set a clear expectation that my campaign would never discuss polls, on or off the record. Voters couldn't give a shit, and the expectations management stuff often comes back to bite you.

A lot of the pollsters in Michigan are herdy and/or shitty. But it's a legit hard race to poll. Black voters, especially working-class Black voters, can be hard to reach. Young voters may be underrepresented in traditional surveys, but now we've mostly shifted to online panels.

The implied projection from prediction markets is El-Sayed eventually winning by ~4, though a larger win or a Stevens win remain possible.

That would reflect a pretty big polling error, though I doubt AES will care so long as he wins.

To get a little meta here, a narrow El-Sayed win would be in the maximal "second-guessing zone" where the establishment will question whether it could have won if it had done X or Y differently, as opposed to being like "yeah, we suck". But that's getting ahead of ourselves.

I don't think all/most of the left-wing thought leaders hate on Obama. But it tends to be a good indicator for which ones are very badly miscalibrated on public opinion. And/or wanna see the D party lose. Literally something like 95% of Democrats have a favorable view of Obama.

There's some irony in that Hong is in some high percentile for authenticity in a literal sense. She's not backing down much from her previous positions, and her affect is not very politican-y. Nearly everyone from DSA to MAGA wants performative "authenticity" though.

It's worth remembering that Congressional races are much more correlated with presidential voting than gubernatorial races. And rationally so: a senator affects policy for the entire country, and the Senate is basically a parliamentary body now. Not true for governors.

Upshot: a flawed gubernatorial candidate is less likely to be given a pass by voters than a flawed senate candidate. People might vote for AES even if they think he's too far left because they don't want Trump to control the Senate. But Hong doesn't benefit from that dynamic.

I feel like there's an increasing amount of cope when an establishment candidate loses to a progressive to just say, "Oh, they were obviously a weak candidate, a different/better establishment candidate would have won."

Certainly, progressive/DSA candidates aren't winning every primary. And there's some cherry-picking in which races get media coverage. But I think it's pretty hard to argue that, say, Stevens (who hasn't lost *yet* to be fair) is a bad candidate from first principles.
